Urbanus (Urbane)
ur-BAY-nus (UR-bayn)
proper noun
From the Latin urbanus, “of the city, refined, courteous,” from urbs, a city.

📖 Biblical Definition

Urbanus — rendered “Urbane” in the Authorized Version — is greeted by Paul as “our helper in Christ.” The change of pronoun is striking: where Paul calls Amplias “my beloved,” he calls Urbane “our helper,” a fellow-worker shared by the whole apostolic company. The Greek word behind “helper” is the same root from which we get the title of a fellow laborer, one who toils alongside in the gospel. Urbane was no spectator in the early church but a working hand, a man who put his shoulder to the common task of spreading and serving the Word. The name, like Amplias, was common among Roman slaves and freedmen, and so again we meet a humble saint exalted by his usefulness in Christ. The Reformed reader notes that Urbane is honored not for office or eloquence but for help — the unglamorous, indispensable labor that keeps gospel work moving forward. The kingdom advances on the backs of such helpers, men who carry, mend, host, fund, and serve without seeking the front. Urbane appears only here, his single verse a testimony that faithful helping is never forgotten by the Lord whose work it serves. His name calls the church to value the laborer over the celebrity, and to count it honor enough to be reckoned a helper in Christ.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A believer at Rome, KJV “Urbane,” whom Paul greets as “our helper in Christ,” a shared fellow-worker in the gospel.

expand to see more

URBANE, the KJV rendering of Urbanus, a Christian at Rome greeted by Paul.

Called “our helper in Christ Jesus” (Rom 16:9).

The plural “our” marks him a fellow-worker of the whole apostolic company.

The name, common among Roman slaves and freedmen, means “of the city.”

He is honored for gospel labor, not for office or eloquence (Rom 16:9).

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 16:9 — "Salute Urbane, our helper in Christ, and Stachys my beloved."

1Co 3:9 — "For we are labourers together with God: ye are God’s husbandry, ye are God’s building."

Php 2:25 — "Yet I supposed it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier, but your messenger, and he that ministered to my wants."

3Jo 1:8 — "We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The lesson to recover is the high worth of the gospel helper — the unseen fellow-worker whose labor advances Christ’s kingdom.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Urbane is the dignity of helping. He bears no title but “helper,” yet that word names the very sinew of gospel work. The kingdom moves forward on the toil of such men — those who carry, host, fund, mend, and serve, asking no recognition and seeking no front rank.

The modern church often prizes the visible gift over the hidden labor, but Scripture honors Urbane for nothing more than help in Christ. His one verse rebukes the cult of the platform. To be a faithful helper is to be a labourer together with God, and the Lord who employs such hands forgets none of their work.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Latin urbanus, “belonging to the city, polished, courteous,” springs from urbs, a city.

expand to see more

Urbanus — Latin for “of the city, refined,” from urbs, city.

KJV “Urbane” differs from the slug-form “Urbanus,” the original Latin.

A common name among Roman freedmen and slaves.

“Helper” renders the Greek synergos, a fellow-worker or co-laborer.

The English word “urbane” (courteous) descends from the same Latin root.

Usage

"The deacon labored as an Urbane, a quiet helper in Christ who sought no notice."

"Paul honored Urbane not for words but for work, calling him “our helper in Christ.”"

"Every congregation depends on the Urbanes who serve without seeking the front."
